speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank my colleague for a very good question. For the banks to say that there is no free lunch-of all groups in Canadian society to say that-is silly. The banks have been one of the most privileged groups in the country. They get special rights from Parliament as contained in the Bank Act. They have been allowed to accumulate an amazing amount of wealth and power, especially on a per capita basis, more than the American banks have. We have allowed them to develop into an almost monopolistic position in this country. They were described by the consumer groups as an oligarchy. For the banks to say there is no free ride, is a little amusing. The banks have paid very little and in some years no tax at all on the hundreds of millions of dollars profit. If anyone is having a free ride in Canada it is the banks.
My colleague mentioned the Third World losses which the banks will experience. That is true. But again, those losses all become tax deductible. Even if the banks are taxed at the 50 per cent level, half of those losses will be paid for by the Canadian taxpayer. If one looks at the profits the banks have made and the dividends they have been paying out one will see that there have been no substantial decreases in dividends. In fact, the banks' profits have been up even though they have been writing down and are potentially in a position of writing off many Third World losses.
The type of financial world that Governments in part have created has been to the benefit of the banks. I remember as a youngster working in a clothing store. On Saturday I would get paid in cash. Now almost everyone is paid by cheque, and that is a help to the banks. Low-income Canadians, the young and the old, do not have big amounts in their banks. They are the ones who suffer the high charges under the banking system.
In committee we proposed having basic accounts without charges for certain people. For the banks to say that poor people, old and young people and those on low incomes should not expect something free from the banks is somewhat obscene and shows insensitivity. It shows that the banks do not realize or appreciate the tremendous benefits they get from doing business. Banks do not seem to be willing at all to help share the wealth they have gained by helping out low-income Canadians by providing a no frills, free bank account-type of business.

speechtext:
There is a procedure of which all Members are aware for moving concurrence in a committee report, and that procedure is provided for under Standing Order 56(1 )(b). Indeed, at any time, an Hon. Member is within his or her rights to move concurrence in a report. However, there has been parliamentary reform introduced into this House, and I would argue that bringing this motion forward today is inappropriate for several reasons.
First, under Standing Order 99(2), the committee can ask the Minister to respond in Parliament to the report. Indeed, the committee has asked the Minister to respond, and the Minister has indicated that he will respond in the House on Tuesday of next week. Since parliamentary reform has taken place, to the best of my knowledge, this is the first time any member of any committee has tried to move concurrence in a report before the Minister has given the ministerial response to the report. There have been instances of concurrence being moved following the Minister's response, and indeed, members of the Finance Committee have moved concurrence in a report following a Minister's response to bring onto the floor of the House of Commons the fact that they are dissatisfied or wish to proceed with this argument.
The second reason it is inappropriate is that we do not require an opposition day to do this. Indeed, while I did not raise this as a point of order today, I believe, had it been challenged, that the Speaker might well have found that today's motion was out of order. I refer specifically to Standing Order 82(3) which reads:
Opposition motions on allotted days may be moved only by Members in opposition to the government and may relate to any matter within the jurisdiction of the Parliament of Canada and also may be used for the purpose of considering reports from standing committees relating to the consideration of estimates therein.
This Standing Order is quite clear that it is foreseen that opposition Parties may choose to use their allotted days to move concurrence in a committee report which deals with the Estimates, but there is no indication in the Standing Order that it should be used for today's particular purpose.
I indicated that I might have been willing to make such a procedural argument, but I did not because I think it is important that we have the opportunity to discuss this report today. The Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) was the first speaker on this motion today, and in his introductory remarks, he raised another ambiguity which has to do with the motion, and that is exactly what we would be voting on if we were to vote in support of this motion.
The Hon. Member for Nickel Belt indicated on several occasions during his speech that he was seeking approval of the report including the recommendations made by members of the New Democratic Party in that report. One of those

recommendations is that the Government place a freeze on all bank service charges with the exception of those prohibited by the Finance Committee majority report for one year effective on the date of this report's tabling in Parliament. The Hon. Of course, neither members of the Liberal Party or of the Conservative Party could support those particular recommendations when we put together the report.
There is an argument that today's motion should be acceptable to government Members because, after all, government Members endorsed the vast majority of the report, which of course they did. However, the NDP Member who moved the motion today has tried to take it one step further and has indicated that he views his motion as encompassing his recommendations, and he said so on several occasions.
There is another reason, of course, why I view this motion as being inappropriate, and that is that the House is already seized of the majority report. There is a Bill standing in my name to this effect. I would like to review what is in the majority report because I think it is important that consumers know what the Finance Committee is pressing for. The first area has to do with information, getting notification and disclosure of what on earth is happening. Certainly the Conservative Members on the committee are committed to the free market system. We recognize that the only way a free market system can work is if customers can actually find out what the costs are of the services which they wish to buy.
First, when a customer opens an account at a deposit-taking institution, he must be told the complete list of charges applicable to that account. It does not seem too radical that you are actually told what is going to be charged.

Second, regardless of what form the bank or trust company makes the consumer sign, waiving his rights, there is a provision in the Bill standing in my name saying they cannot waive the rights to protection under the Bank Act. Third, there is established a consumer-complaint procedure, first at the branches, and then at the head offices. Finally, if the consumer cannot achieve simple justice, the bank has an obligation to notify the customer of the right to take the complaint to the Superintendent of Financial Institutions to have the Superintendent pursue the complaint on the customer's behalf.
In addition, there is a requirement that the Superintendent report annually to Parliament on the nature and number of complaints that are received by him, and how they were resolved. What we have provided for, in addition, is that when fees are about to change, the bank or trust company, the deposit taking institution, has a choice of how they notify the customer. They can do it directly in writing, in which case there is a 30-day advance period, or they can post notices, prominent notices, in the bank branch. If they don't contact the client directly, they have to post the notice 60 days in advance. This all designed to ensure that the customer has available to him or her a complete list of the charges so that if they see a charge that they do not like, they know well enough in advance that they can move the money to another institution.
Supply
There are a number of practices occurring among deposit taking institutions which the committee feels should be prohibited, as they are against the public interest. The first of these is charging for closing an account after the account has been opened for a long period of time.
It is the feeling of the committee that if we are to have an efficient system where consumers can indeed shop, they should have the right to take their money out of the bank and indeed shop with it rather than having a deterrent-fee levied on that account simply because they want their money back.
The second type of transaction which we found repugnant was the concept of charging consumers for not doing anything. We didn't have a particular problem with charging the consumers for utilizing the bank services, writing cheques and things like that. We did find the practice was creeping in of charging consumers for not doing something, after they had not written any cheques or made any deposits for a year, or for a matter of months in some cases. We felt that these practices should be prohibited. After all, if the money is just sitting there, the bank is earning interest on that money. The fact that you don't cause the bank any work should not be a reason for it to levy a charge.
We have had no problem whatsoever with banks or trust companies charging people who wrote NSF cheques. When we get to the person who deposits an NSF cheque, this person is already a victim a victim of the person who wrote the NSF cheque. We do not feel the deposit taking institution should apply a further penalty on the depositor. If they are going to collect money, let them collect every cent that it cost them to cover the transactions with the bounced cheque by charging the person who wrote the cheque.
Similarly, banks have recently introduced charges simply because the balance is small. We think this should be prohibited. On savings accounts, the bank do nothing. It does not process cheques or send out monthly statements. The money is left in the bank. The bank should not apply a charge to a consumer just because there is a low balance.
In summary, to incorporate these recommendations, we have recommended prohibiting five specific transactions. We have recommended that a basic or lifeline account be established for those of modest means who have modest needs in the banking system. We would allow up to six deposits or withdrawals monthly without any charge for maintaining the fee with this basic account. The reaction of the banks has been fairly extreme on this. They suggested that allowing people to have the right to make deposits and withdrawals-a very small number, six a month-is somehow requiring them to offer free banking.
These are the types of accounts that the banks lived on for the first hundred years in this country. To the best of my recollection, at no time during those hundred years were the banks ever registered as charities.

Since 1923 the maximum fine which could be imposed for noncompliance by the banks has been $1,000. Obviously, $1,000 is worth a lot more in today's dollars. Therefore, the majority report recommends that if banks do not comply with the recommendations of the committee in the future, they should be subject to a fine of up to $10,000 for the first occurrence- that is the shot across the bow-and, if they continue to repeat within a three-year period, to a fine of up to $100,000.
In summary, I will give my full support to the majority report of the committee. However, the motion standing in the name of the Member for Nickel Belt is premature, ill-advised, and possibly procedurally destructive of the parliamentary reform process because of the timing and the way in which the motion is put.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the committee commissioned a report from Dr. Terry Thomas, an economist, with the Library of Parliament, on this specific subject. Banks, of course, have available to them essentially two sources of profit. One is the spread on interest rates and the second is service charge fees.
We found that the rate of increase of service charge fees had been averaging nearly 17 per cent a year, considerably in excess of the rate of inflation or the rate of transaction growth. We also found that while the combination of interest spreads and service fees had remained stable for many years, giving a legitimate argument to the banks that as they raised service fees they were decreasing their interest margins, in 1987, the year in which all the complaints arose, there was in fact a quantum jump in the total profitability of the banks.
The combination of the interest spread fees and the service charge fees jumped total bank profitability on Canadian operations by 35 per cent over 1986 and the profit on Canadian operations in 1987 was the highest recorded since we have been keeping statistics. It is, therefore, no wonder that bank consumers were very aware that this massive increase in service charges was going through.
One additional thing occurred. We also commissioned a study on domestic profitability versus profitability on foreign operations. We found it very interesting to observe that while historically the profit on foreign operations had been large and sustained, in 1987 there was a very sharp drop in the profitability on foreign operations which just happened to offset the very large jump in domestic operations. There was roughly a
35 per cent jump in charges to Canadian consumers per $100 of assets administered and at the same time there just happened to be a drop of 25 per cent per $100 of assets administered in the foreign branch. Over-all, the total profitability of the bank per $100 of assets administered was virtually unchanged from the year before.
So there certainly appears to be a case to question whether that rise in the charges on Canadian operations was not introduced in part to offset the losses which were occurring particularly from South American and Third World loans.

They have shown a good deal of political initiative in this area and have, as in other areas, been innovative and prepared for the committee to take its own line. It has been clear for some time that the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) would much prefer that the committee do something else than look at the question of bank charges. They would much prefer that the committee simply scold the banks and then go away, to be deep sixed until after the next election, and hopefully never see the light of day again.
The Member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McCrossan) and the Member for Mississauga North (Mr. Blenkarn) and others on the committee are not known for kowtowing to the Minister of Finance and the Minister of State for Finance. Those Members have taken an independent line on such issues as deregulation of financial institutions and banking centres, as well as on other matters. That is why I am puzzled that their courage seems to have suddenly run out in this particular case, and they have decided not to support this motion to concur in the report of the committee.
It is not true that this procedure has not been done before. My colleague, the Member for Nickel Belt moved concurrence in a report on the unemployment insurance system which came unanimously from the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigrant prior to having had a response from the Minister. Furthermore, our motion allows the House of Commons as a whole to state our opinion about the way the banks have been gouging Canadians steadily in the last few years by the unsupportable and unsustainable increases in service charges. A simple debate on concurrence which is permitted under the rules of the House does not lead to a vote and would not have the same force in sending the message to the banks that they have been singularly asinine in their reaction to the concerns of Canadians as reflected by the committee.
Monday will be the final day on which to deal with the question of Supply and the Estimates. It is a parliamentary tradition dating back to the Magna Carta that the grievances of the citizens are heard by Parliament before Supply is voted. Banking is a federal responsibility in this country and citizens have a real grievance with respect to the performance of the banks. The federal Government has the power to stop the gouging, the deception and misinformation. It has the power to ensure that the banks deal honestly and fairly with their clients and customers. I do not know of another grievance that is as legitimate as that for airing at this time.
I am concerned that the Government Members, most of whom come from the Finance Committee, are continuing an
elaborate web of explanation in order to vote directly contrary to that which they purport to support in the unanimous report of the Finance Committee. While the Government Members talk tough, I daresay they are turning into wimps. That is unfortunate.

The New Democrats raised the issue of interest rates in the early 1980s, and fought on the issue of the unfair retail credit card rates. That issue continues to persist. New Democrats fought on the issue of bank profits. We complained that the chartered banks had made profits of hundreds of millions of dollars but paid no tax on those profits.
When we have talked about the abuse of oligopoly of power by the chartered banks, on many occasions we have done so alone. Finance and Economic Affairs well and if he is a socialist, then I would have to abandon my Party, and I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that there will be no need for me to do so.

This esteemed lobbyist has attacked the press, particularly the Toronto Star. He has suggested that everyone makes a few mistakes and the press is simply dealing in horror stories. He has not recognized the anger that is out there among Canadians. As the committee put it, one of the major reasons for all this is that there is a whole generation of Canadians of the age, perhaps, of the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) and myself, who were brought up to trust the banks. There was not a lot of variety of financial institutions in those days. When I started a bank account, it was with the Toronto Dominion Bank some time in the 1940s. I fully expected to stay with that bank for most of my life at the time and did so, in fact, for something like 20 or 25 years until I became so annoyed with the way they were dealing with me as a customer that I switched to another bank.
I have to say that for all the courtesies I receive from the other bank that from time to time I have problems. For me, as a Member of Parliament, someone with perhaps a larger income and more financial dealings than many Canadians, it is difficult to know who the devil is in charge. I also get these quixotic service charges from time to time. I have found that if I go to the bank and pound my fist on the table a couple of times, I can get the charge reversed. I think bank managers have that particular discretion. But that is not a privilege that is available to a lot of Canadians. They feel afraid to do it. They feel they are in the grip of the banks and because they are powerless they feel this frustration and anger which has grown and grown.
There have been a number of cases cited. One of the cases is about a woman who was charged $2 to convert a $20 bill into change so she could go to the launderette. She was a woman who eventually got so mad she called up my constituency office. After this matter was raised the transaction was reversed. The bank said: "Gee, I guess someone made a mistake". But these cases are not mistakes if they occur and reoccur. What is happening, of course, is that the banks are being hypocritical on this particular subject. They have given instructions to the local branch managers to improve their fee income without much regard as to how that would take place. Senior managers have blinded themselves. They have covered their faces and told their subordinates: "Go ahead and do it, but if you get caught apologize and turn it around".
A case came into my office just the other day from a student who lives in my constituency. She had problems with the Bank of Montreal just across the street from Parliament Hill. She gave her landlord a post-dated cheque for her July rent because she was going on holiday sometime in June. When she came back from holiday she found out that the cheque had

bounced. It had been presented by the landlord, possibly in error, prior to the time for which it was dated. The bank had refused to honour it and, therefore, there was a $6 charge and the cheque went NSF. When the student complained that it was the bank's mistake, she was told by the bank's customer service officer that the banks do not check the date on cheques under $1,000. I deal with that particular bank and they have never told me that they do not check the date on post-dated cheques that are under $1,000. That raises the question of what kind of service it is when those people who can afford to write cheques for $1,000 or more receive one service from the bank and those people who cannot receive another service.
That particular $6 charge was refunded after we spoke to the bank manager. We were told that the charge that was imposed does represent the usual practice. In other words, it is not even a mistake in this particular case, it is the usual practice. How was the public to find that out? They would find out when they were dinged by the bank.

Without any instructions, the bank had begun to cover the overdraft on their account not by a transfer from their savings account, which had been the practice in the past, but by transfer from their Visa account. They had not even been able to find out what was happening with the Visa account unless they went to the money machine. This was a person who was seeking to manage his financial affairs so as not to pile up a lot of credit card charges, but here was an unannounced change in policy by the bank which hurt that particular constituent.

service, I would assume, on behalf of all Canadians, particularly as we move into a cashless society, they would not tolerate that kind of competition and would provide a service that was sufficiently adequate.
I have to accept that the banks are not the only villains in this particular piece. The constituent went to the bank and said: "Well, would you please stop collecting that money. According to the court order you have your pound of flesh, you have your money". The bank refused. It refused for about four months running, through the late winter and spring of this year until finally just a few days ago matters came to a head. By that time the bank had received several thousand dollars more than was its due, according to the court order. The constituent finally went to the bank and said: 'Enough is enough. If you won't deal with this, then I am going to talk to my Member of Parliament. I am going to talk to the press. I will raise it with the newspapers in places such as Toronto, Montreal and Ottawa. That kind of excuse will not wash any more. We need to get away from a situation in which millions of Canadians have to come to their Member of Parliament in order to get redress in such cases.
The bank fee for service income has been by about 19 per cent per annum. This represents a 10 per cent or 11 per cent increase in the level of rates. Banks have been having about a 7 per cent increase in their volume of business. The cost of doing business has been going up at about the same rate as their volume of business, about 7 per cent. They are benefiting in terms of more efficient operations because of computerization, the public not seeing that. The public is being charged more and more and more.
It is as though I went to The Bay to buy a suit and I had to pay $2 to get in, $1 to ride upstairs on the escalator, $20 an hour for the sales clerk for consulting fees while deciding what suit to buy, a charge to have the suit fixed, another delivery charge to have it delivered to my home, and something else when I went out the door to leave the place. I believe that they have obligations to the people of Canada in return for the enormous privileges and profitability that they enjoy because of the charter they have from the Government of Canada through this Parliament.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-BANK CHARGES-CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
We know that all those who deal with financial institutions have a stake in knowing that their interests are well served. They are all affected by service charges. It would be an error to think that this is a minor issue, and some of the credit for ensuring that no one can stand aside on it is due to the work of the committee.
Let me begin by looking briefly at the context in which this whole question has arisen. We need to have a firm understanding of the issue and the full implications of any possible action before accepting any detailed recommendations. We also have to understand the recent history of the financial services industry and the way it has developed in recent years.
This Government has a proud record of action in defence of consumer rights. We have consistently put it as one of the goals of our reform of the financial institution sector. Legislation has already been passed by Parliament to implement the first stages of that reform. A significant part of the package contributed to strengthening the protection of consumers, depositors and policy holders. Still further measures are part of the remaining legislation on financial institution reform as has been clear since the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) released his draft of the new trust and loans company Bill last December. These measures will go even further to protect consumers from conflicts of interest and will encourage competition. They will ensure that the present high standard of corporate behaviour is enhanced in the interests of all those who participate in the financial system, which are most Canadians.
There is a valid role for Government in ensuring that individuals are treated fairly. When we look at how that responsibility has been carried out in the past, it is fairly clear that the existing provisions in the Bank Act and in regulations do not go far enough. They need to be updated to take account of current conditions. At the same time we must be careful not to go too far with regulation. Unnecessary detailed regulations must be avoided. Instead, we must remember that market competition is the best way to obtain fair pricing practices.
I want to note that competition has already produced positive changes for consumers in certain institutions. We also must emphasize that disclosure of information is the foundation of the effective exercise of consumers' rights. Disclosure enables individuals to exercise their own rights without having to rely on the Government. I want to return to this in a few moments.
One key element in understanding why service charges are before us today is the recent history of the financial industry. I want to very briefly go over some of the key points in the way the industry has been developing. We all remember the days when there were no service charges for most bank services at banks-at least I remember that. Of course, there was very

June 23, 1988
Supply
little interest paid on deposits because, as we all know, the banks used the difference between what they earned from deposits and what they paid to depositors to cover their expenses.
Those were also the days when you had a simple choice going into a bank. You could have a chequing account or a savings account. On one you got next to no interest even in nominal terms, and on the other you had the privilege of depositing in person and making withdrawals in person. You also had a simple choice of where to bank. Outside the big cities you could go to whichever of the one or two or three chartered banks had a branch near you. In the cities the choice was larger. There might be a branch of each of the big banks near you. If a local trust company had a branch, you might be able to use it for some services. If your province had established a savings bank with a local branch, you could go there, or if you lived near a credit union you could get some banking services there also. But that was about it. The point I am making is that in the last two or three decades the financial services system has changed enormously. The number of choices each participant in the system has to make has multiplied many times. There is vastly increased flexibility, and there is far greater capacity to get the services that you need. There is also much greater competition.
The trust companies, and we now have many more trust companies operating across the country, are into the provision of service and what amounts to direct competition with the major chartered banks. Credit unions have grown in number and are also offering a far wider selection of options. Today as a consumer of financial services, you have a choice of institutions. You are not limited to just one bank even in small communities. You have a choice of instruments. The two or three types of accounts of 20 years ago have been replaced by dozens of types of accounts with different terms and conditions and with different advantages. You are not even limited anymore to bankers' hours. The automatic tellers machines and competition between institutions has brought Canadians longer hours of service, Saturday service and, in many areas, 24 hours a day service.
There is always a price to pay for improvements on this scale, and in the case of the financial system more competition and more choices for consumers has meant greater complexity and a much more elaborate infrastructure. But most of us benefit very considerably from the new situation. I have heard no widespread demand that we go back 30 years. I do not believe that the people want that. I know that our economic health would be considerably impaired by any attempt to return to the simpler, but less flexible, less adaptable, less competitive system of an earlier period that I remember so well. As there is therefore no going back, the question is only about how we pay for what we get.
Specifically, do we extend the "user-pay" principle which enables individuals to "buy" the services they need, or do we revert to a system which spreads the cost of all services over all customers? Or do we recognize that no single approach is
appropriate in this less than perfect world and look for a solution that combines elements of both approaches?
The committee report has left us in no doubt about what has happened, and it describes very accurately the process that has brought us to where we are today. Let me quote very briefly at this point from the report itself which reads:
The Committee is not interested in turning back the clock. In principle
explicit pricing is a welcome development.
The committee has accepted that greater choice must be paid for, and that service charges by and large make an acceptable and appropriate contribution to the cost of doing business.
The committee has highlighted flaws in the system, at least in terms of the requirements for disclosure. It has brought to our attention that the present system does not always work without error or mistake. It has indeed pointed to specific cases where obvious injustice has occurred, either because of individual mistakes or because an institution's system has been too rigid.
The Government's proposals have to take into account that the basic system is sound and not in need of major structural changes. Whatever is wrong will not be fixed by forcing the whole system backward. We do not want to interfere needlessly in one aspect of the sector's activities.
We also have to take into account what in the sector has caused the confusion and problems. It is perfectly clear that the real problems arise from a lack of communications. I say that without in any way denying that mistakes and wrong decisions may have been made, and I do not mean to suggest either that the problem is not real, that it is a question of how we look at it and that a good public relations job will make everyone happy. That would obviously be very wrong.
I do mean that when we listen to the people on the street or the people who have been writing to the offices of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), the Minister of State for Finance and individual Members of Parliament, including the Hon. Member for Edmonton East (Mr. Lesick) and me, the biggest question we hear is: "How was I supposed to know what the financial institution was going to do to me"? The cry, heard over and over again, is: "I just didn't know".
We can all appreciate the problem. People must know when they have choices, and must have sufficient information to make their choices. They must have the proper information to allow them to shop around to find the best deal possible and to take advantage of the options and flexibilities now provided by the system, and of which the system is justly proud.
This is basic to any idea of natural justice. It is fundamental to any system of free enterprise and free competition. So, as I said at the outset of these comments, we come to disclosure and we come also to the thorny question of the best way to ensure that full and proper disclosure occurs.
June 23, 1988

The Government does not believe that it is all black or white. Beyond a certain point, we cannot force people to learn or understand what they need to know. Beyond a certain point, we cannot effectively force institutions to do things without interfering to an unacceptable degree in their activities. We have to find a way that combines elements of prescribed regulations with good corporate citizenship.
It is in the institutions' own interests, after all, to have contented customers. It would be unprofitable for institutions to offer new options to customers, to attract them and then to alienate them by clumsy or careless provision of essential information. It would be curiously short-sighted for any institution which is based on dealing with people and selling them services fundamental to the operation of our economic system in the long term to write off one group in society or one potential customer.
I think it is quite reasonable to talk about options and possible ways to proceed, so long as we do not talk ourselves into impractical or unreasonable corners. We must not base an entire system of regulation on admitted injustices or absurdities, though we must strenuously work toward a system without such flaws.
We must recognize that there is a great diversity in the practices of institutions, a diversity which benefits their customers, and we must be careful not to legislate or regulate that diversity away. We have to remember that past experience teaches us to be leery of the practicality or benefits of any system of controls on prices and fees.
The Minister of State for Finance has made clear a number of times that the Government's response to the committee report will be forthcoming as quickly as possible, and hopefully by the end of this month. The Government's action, when it comes, will be developed after considering the interests of both the institutions and the customers in the system.
In shaping these proposals, the Government will benefit considerably from the work of the committee. We will be moving as quickly as possible to correct errors in the system and to ensure that the customers of our financial institutions are equipped with the information they need.
I regret very much that the Opposition has made this a partisan issue, and needlessly divided the support this House should be giving to the committee's goal of better protection for the customers of financial institutions.

Mr. Speaker, I want to first compliment the Hon. Member for his well documented speech. I think we all enjoyed going down memory lane about how the banking system developed. I think it is important to remember where we were and how far we have come in the banking system.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a couple of brief comments with regard to the question that is before us today. I would remind Hon. Members that we are dealing here with an opposition motion

June 23, 1988
Supply
that is not to be considered a question of confidence in the Government, because we want to maintain the non-partisan debate that came about as a result of the recommendations of the Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs. That committee was able to make recommendations with regard to bank charges that were supported by all three political Parties.
I want to briefly note the kinds of problems that led the committee to investigate what the banks were doing. Here is one simple example. The Bank of Nova Scotia at 225 Red River Road, Thunder Bay, for example, charges 40 cents for each deposit into an account that has a minimum balance of less than $500. Here, we have banks charging customers to deposit their money in their own accounts.
A second example is in the riding of Oshawa. Mrs. Yvonne Mitchelldeck of Ajax was upset because her Toronto-Domin-ion Bank branch at the Pickering Town Centre had charged her babysitter $5 to cash a $45 cheque. Here is a bank charging a young babysitter $5 to cash a cheque of $45. These kinds of shocking incidents is what motivated the Finance Committee to investigate the kinds of user-fees or service fees that the banks have been laying on people as of late.
Having studied this problem and the fact that banks are charging people for basic banking services, the committee came up with some recommendations. I do not want to go into the details of them, but they said that basic banking services ought to be available to people. You ought to have a right to a basic bank account. You ought to be able to deposit money in your account. You ought to be able to have a small balance. You ought to be able to have an inactive account. You ought to be able to close out an account without getting dinged, without getting an extra fee laid on you. Those are important recommendations.
These recommendations really come out of one basic principle, and that is a question about money, whether money is a public good or simply a private product, a private commodity. The banks are treating money-and their services are a part of what money is-as simply a private commodity, that they can sell willy-nilly, without considering the interest of the community, and that they can charge anybody as much or as often as they would like to. I would like to suggest that money is a public good. The dollar bill is something that was established by the Crown. The dollar bill is not some private thing that a banker can go around and sell. In effect, that is what they are doing when they charge you a fee to deposit money in your own account, or charge you an enormous amount to cash a cheque. They are treating the dollar bill as their private plaything. I think that is a fundamental mistake.
We are being challenged on that to say: "Where do you guys stand with regard to the nationalization of banks? Aren't you really going to nationalize all the Canadian banks? Isn't that the real problem?" No. That is a red herring. If you want to talk about public versus private interest with regard to money,
you ought to ask how come banks over the last couple of decades have been able to privatize the dollar? That in effect is what they have done. What they have done is create something which is very popular, something which we all use and that is the credit card.
I have a Visa credit card with the Commerce. They have managed over the last few decades to privatize the dollar. They charge us enormous interest rates for using these cards, using what is a public good.
The central, fundamental question here is whether or not money is a public good or whether it is a private plaything. We ought to congratulate the Finance Committee for waking up and responding to the complaints of ordinary Canadians who are saying that they want to get the banks off their backs and that they want the banks to remember that they have a service to deliver. They are not only there to make a profit-and goodness knows they make enough of that-but they are there to provide a basic service, that is to assist the Canadian people in the circulation of money, and to help us in meeting our basic needs.
I just wanted to remind this House that the Finance Committee was doing the right thing when it started to investigate these exorbitant fees. There is a public interest when it comes to money, and there is a public interest when it comes to banks, and that public interest has to be represented by this House. We ought to vote in favour of this resolution.

I will be very brief, Mr. Speaker. I wonder if you might consider, before we vote on Monday, making a ruling on whether or not this is a motion of confidence. I suggest that only the Government itself can decide whether or not a certain vote is a motion of confidence. I remember, before I came to this House in 1968, in February of that year, the Pearson Government was defeated on a Finance Bill. That was interpreted by Mr. Pearson not to be a confidence vote. He came back before the House a day or two later and moved a motion of confidence in his Government. He specified that that was the confidence vote.
Another thing, when the Government of Joe Clark was defeated in December, 1979, he was defeated on a subamendment proposed by our Party, and the Prime Minister that day deemed that to be a confidence motion. I see in the House now the Assistant Government House Leader. I think the only way that this would be a confidence vote is if the Government House Leader, or the Assistant Government House Leader, or the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), were to get up and deem that this indeed was a confidence vote. Only the Government itself, according to our practices and our customs of this country, in the British Parliamentary system, can decide whether something is a confidence vote or not. Perhaps the Speaker can get up and confirm that that is a proper interpretation of our rules. According to our practices I am quite sure that it is.
If this is not a confidence motion it may make it a lot easier for Members of the House of Commons to get up in unison and support this report of the Finance Committee. This report
Supply
was supported by Members of all three political Parties. The motion is very clear. My friend from Nickel Belt does not consider this to be a confidence motion, nor do other Members on the opposition side.
If we can get that confirmation from the responsible government Minister, then this is indeed not a motion of nonconfidence. It might be useful, Mr. Speaker, if you could comment on whether my interpretation of the rules is correct and proper.
I want to make one more point which may not be relevant to the debate. The Member for Okanagan-Similkameen (Mr. King) said that this was similar to a Liberal motion on NATO. That Liberal motion on NATO did not specify that it was not a confidence motion. At that time the Government made it clear that it interpreted the motion to be one of non-confidence. Therefore, that was altogether different than the case today.
Would you, Mr. Speaker, be kind enough to confirm that, according to our practices and traditions, this is not a motion of non-confidence and the only way it would be is if the Government were to indicate in a very clear way that it considers this motion to be one of non-confidence in the Government.

Mr. Speaker, if I may, I will address a few remarks to this particular point. We have had a very useful debate on the issue of the nineteenth Report of the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs respecting bank charges. However, I would suggest to my hon. friend and the House that the House may have voted unanimously if my hon. friend had taken the course of action open to him, that is, to move under Motions on the Order Paper that the House concur in the committee's report. That may very well have received the unanimous consent of the House and would have sent the message to the Government which my hon. friend sought.
Second, I have not examined the report in detail as other Members of the House will have, but I do understand that there is a minority report of the NDP included in it which may confuse the House as to exactly what it was voting for. Members on the government side, at least, may not have been sure whether they were voting for all of the things the committee recommended and/or the items recommended by the New Democratic Party.
Finally, we adopt the position of the previous Government with respect to this particular order. We will be moving ourselves on things of this nature, perhaps imminently. We do not want to make history for my hon. friend. For that reason we will be considering this a matter of confidence and the Government will be voting against the motion. Our position on bank charges has been made clear by the majority members of the committee.
